questionText:
An undirected, unweighted, simple graph $G(V, E)$ is said to be 2-colorable if there exists a function $c: V \rightarrow \{0, 1\}$ such that for every $(u, v) \in E, c(u) \neq c(v)$.

Which of the following statements about 2-colorable graphs is/are true?
options: If $G$ is 2-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of odd length
If $G$ is 2-colorable, then $G$ may contain cycles of even length
An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is 2-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|V| + |E|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list
An optimal algorithm for testing whether $G$ is 2-colorable runs in time $\Theta(|E| \log |V|)$, if $G$ is represented as an adjacency list
explanation:
Step 1: Understand 2-Colorable Graphs (Bipartite Graphs).
A graph $G$ is 2-colorable if and only if it is bipartite. By Koenig's Theorem, a graph is bipartite (2-colorable) if and only if it contains no cycles of odd length.

Step 2: Evaluate Statements A and B.
- Since a 2-colorable graph cannot have any odd cycles, Statement A is false.
- A 2-colorable graph can contain cycles of even length (for instance, a cycle graph $C_4$ is 2-colorable). Thus, Statement B is true.

Step 3: Evaluate Statements C and D.
- 2-colorability can be tested by traversing the graph using Breadth-First Search (BFS) or Depth-First Search (DFS). For an adjacency list representation, BFS/DFS inspects all vertices and edges in $\Theta(|V| + |E|)$ time, which is optimal.
- Therefore, Statement C is true and Statement D is false.

Hence, options B and C are true.
